title: Deck Shuffler With Reset
statement:
Build a class that holds an array of distinct integers and can shuffle it fairly.

  • Shuffler(nums) stores the starting array.
  • shuffle() returns a random ordering of the values as a new array. Every one of the n! orderings must be equally likely on every call, no matter what was returned before.
  • reset() returns the array in its original starting order.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the object. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor). Because shuffle is random, any permutation is accepted for a single call. Long runs of shuffle on a small array are also checked for fairness: each ordering, and each value at each position, must show up about as often as chance predicts.

examples.why: Each shuffle may return any of the 6 orderings (these two are one possible run). reset always gives back [4, 8, 15].
Repeating an ordering is fine. A shuffle that always swaps would never return [1, 2], and that is not fair.

constraints: At most 10 000 calls to shuffle and reset in total
hints: Sorting with a random comparator looks easy, but it is not uniform. Think about building the shuffled array one slot at a time.
For the last slot, pick one of the n values uniformly at random. For the slot before it, pick one of the n − 1 remaining values, and so on. That gives n! equally likely outcomes.
Fisher–Yates does this in place: for i from n − 1 down to 1, swap a[i] with a[j] where j is uniform in [0, i], including i itself. Work on a copy so reset can return the original.

explain.intuition:
A fair shuffle is a sequence of fair choices. Choose which value goes in the last slot: n options. Then which of the remaining values goes before it: n − 1 options. Each full ordering comes from exactly one sequence of choices, and there are n · (n − 1) · … · 1 = n! sequences, all equally likely.

Fisher–Yates performs those choices in place. The suffix a[i+1..] holds values already placed; the prefix a[0..i] is the pool. Swapping a random pool element into slot i places it and keeps the rest in the pool. The classic bug is picking j from [0, i) instead of [0, i]: a value can then never stay where it is, so some orderings become impossible. The same goes for array.sort(() => Math.random() − 0.5), a frontend favourite that gives visibly biased results.
steps: Store a copy of nums as the original.
reset(): return a copy of the original.
shuffle(): copy the original into a. For i from n − 1 down to 1, pick j uniformly in [0, i] and swap a[i] and a[j].
pitfalls: Choosing j from [0, i) (Sattolo's algorithm). It only produces orderings where every element moves, so [1, 2, 3] can never come back unchanged.
Choosing j from the whole range [0, n) for every i. That gives nⁿ equally likely swap sequences, which cannot split evenly over n! orderings, so the result is biased.
Returning the internal array itself, so a caller who keeps an earlier result sees it change after the next shuffle, or reset returns shuffled data.

solutions.title: Draw from a shrinking pool
solutions.idea: Copy the values into a pool. Repeatedly remove a uniformly random element from the pool and append it to the result.
solutions.time: O(n²) per shuffle (removal shifts the pool)

solutions.title: Fisher–Yates on a copy
solutions.idea: Walk from the end; swap each slot with a random slot at or before it. Every ordering has probability exactly 1/n!.

followups: Show that sort(() => Math.random() − 0.5) is biased for a 3-element array. Which orderings come up too often?
You need a random sample of k items from a stream too large to store. How does reservoir sampling relate to Fisher–Yates?
